newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't backtracks over reform amendment.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't backtracks over reform amendment.

text.p: The Brazilian government has decided to withdraw support for a controversial amendment to its civil service reform bill that would have exempted lawmakers from a proposed pay ceiling, a senior politician said Monday.
"There is no reason for the extra ceiling," said Deputy Michel Temer, the president of the Chamber of Deputies, refering to the amendment.

The clause would have allowed lawmakers, ministers and aides of senior civil servants to collect up to double the 10,800 reais ($10,188) monthly ceiling on pay and pension included in the reform for all others categories of public sector workers.
"The extra-ceiling was widely criticized and the (party) leaders were sensitive to the outcry," Temer told reporters in comments broadcast by the national Globo television network.
The amendment was due to be put to a vote on the floor later this week, probably Wednesday.

Other potentially damaging amendments were also likely to be floated, including one which would strip from the reform a clause allowing for the dismissal of currently unfireable workers, one of the bill's key points.

Congress-watchers said the U-turn might anger leaders of government-allied parties who last week said they would follow the example of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso. He described the amendment as "the price to pay" for civil service reform.
"Now the leaders feel betrayed by the president," wrote political columnist Tales Faria in newspaper O Globo.
"They think he should have faced the music in return for keeping the confidence of allied parties..."
Some commentators suggested last week that a retreat by the government on the amendment might put the reform itself at risk when the bill is put to a second vote in the lower house.

An estimated 140 deputies who earn pensions from previous civil service posts would lose from the original ceiling on pay and pensions. Their votes are essential to the two three- fifths majorities the government needs for approval in the lower house.
But other observers said the strength of public opinion against the exemptions would see the government through.

"This is all part of a political game," said Marcelo Cordeiro. "Do you really think the government was going to let itself be trampled on by half-a-dozen lawmakers who wanted to defend their pensions?"
The government hopes the bill will help reduce Brazil's public sector operational deficit, which was equivalent to 3.89 percent of GDP in 1996.
